1. Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then gradually converges toward true values — suggesting a lag or delayed response to actual market dynamics.

2. After sharp price spikes (e.g., >45.00), model forecasts often overshoot and remain elevated for several days, failing to reflect mean reversion or downward correction — indicating poor handling of volatility clustering or momentum decay.

3. Model exhibits persistent upward bias in the middle-to-late forecast horizon (days 15–30), particularly when true values show downward trends — suggesting failure to capture short-term mean reversion or overconfidence in trend continuation.

4. When true values exhibit sudden drops (e.g., below 35.00), model forecasts remain stubbornly high, failing to adjust — indicating poor sensitivity to regime shifts or policy-driven corrections.

5. Model underestimates true values in the first 5–10 days when historical prices are volatile or show strong downward momentum — suggesting failure to recognize early warning signals or insufficient weight on recent volatility.

6. Model tends to smooth out sharp transitions in true values, treating them as noise — leading to underestimation of sudden drops or overestimation of gradual recoveries.

7. Model performs better when true values are clustered around mid-range (35–45) and worse when prices are extreme (below 30 or above 50) — suggesting calibration issues for outlier regimes.

8. Model shows increasing error variance as forecast horizon extends beyond 20 days — indicating diminishing reliability for long-term predictions, especially when true values exhibit non-linear or regime-switching behavior.
